paper_a.title: HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm

paper_b.title: Probabilistic Counting Algorithms for Data Base Applications

metadata.description: HyperLogLog (Flajolet-Fusy-Gandouet-Meunier 2007) is a direct refinement/extension of Flajolet-Martin's Probabilistic Counting with Stochastic Averaging (PCSA, 1985). Both solve streaming cardinality estimation via bit-pattern observables of hashed values combined with stochastic averaging across m substreams; both rely on Mellin-transform / depoissonization asymptotics. HLL replaces FM's leftmost-zero-of-BITMAP observable (R) with the per-substream maximum leftmost-1-position (Max), and replaces direct averaging by the harmonic mean, trading FM's 0.78/sqrt(m) accuracy with 32-bit-per-register storage for HLL's 1.04/sqrt(m) accuracy at log_2 log_2 N bits per register. HLL explicitly cites FM as prior work (AP313.4) and inherits its analytical machinery.

matches.explanation: Both state the same problem: estimate the cardinality (number of distinct elements) of a streamed multiset M in a single pass with sublinear auxiliary memory. The wording differs slightly (HLL adds the explicit O(log log N) memory target reflecting its tighter bound) but the problem is the canonical streaming-distinct-count problem common to both papers.

Idealized hash function mapping records into uniformly random binary strings. FM splits this across DP314.1 (the practical hash to [0, 2^L-1]) and DP314.6 (the probabilistic model on infinite binary strings B with i.i.d. uniform bits); HLL fuses both into one definition DP313.1. The mathematical content is identical: hashed values are i.i.d. uniform infinite bit strings.

Both define the bit-pattern observable rho(s). HLL uses the LEFTMOST-1 position (number of leading zeros + 1), while FM uses the LEAST-SIGNIFICANT-1 position (number of trailing zeros). Mathematically these are bit-reversed versions of the same geometric statistic; both have the same distribution P[rho >= k] = 2^{1-k}. The two papers' choices reflect different downstream uses (FM accumulates bits in BITMAP[rho], HLL takes the max of rho per bucket), so the role within the algorithm is analogous rather than identical.

Stochastic averaging is the same technique in both papers (HLL's DP313.4 explicitly cites Flajolet-Martin 1985, and is even tagged origin: external in HLL). A single hash is split: leading b bits select one of m=2^b buckets, remaining bits feed the per-bucket observable. This is the central engineering trick of FM and is reused verbatim in HLL.

Per-substream observable. HLL stores Max_j = max_{x in bucket_j} rho(x) (a single integer). FM instead stores the BITMAP vector (DP314.4) and extracts R = position of leftmost zero (DP314.5). Both observables target the same statistic log_2(n_j), but HLL's max is a tight log log N-bit summary while FM's BITMAP+R uses Theta(log N) bits. The conceptual role is the same: a per-substream estimator of bucket cardinality, but the encoding differs.

Cardinality estimator construction. FM uses E = (1/phi) 2^R with phi = 0.77351... (Magic constant DP314.15) on the AVERAGED R (i.e. arithmetic mean of substream maxima, then exponentiate). HLL uses E = alpha_m m^2 / sum_j 2^{-M[j]} (HARMONIC mean of 2^{M_j}) with alpha_m = 1/(2 log 2) approx 0.7213. Conceptually both invert the geometric distribution of the per-bucket observable to recover n; the key methodological novelty in HLL is the harmonic mean replacing FM's geometric (and earlier LogLog's geometric) mean.

The main algorithm. HLL's AP313.1 (analytical) and AP313.2 (practical with small/large-range corrections) parallel FM's AP314.3 (PCSA). Both: single-pass; hash each record; first b bits select bucket alpha; remainder feeds per-bucket observable; final estimate combines per-bucket data via a constant times m * (mean-like aggregate). They differ in the per-bucket observable (BITMAP vs single max register), in the aggregation rule (arithmetic mean of R then 2^{S/m} vs harmonic mean of 2^{M_j}), and in the bias-correction constants (1/phi vs alpha_m). The PCSA-with-small/large-range-corrections aspect of HLL's AP313.2 has no FM analogue (FM-PCSA used a separate L-rule).

Initialize-registers step in both algorithms. FM zeros the BITMAP matrix (ASP314.1, ASP314.4); HLL zeros (or sets to -infty) the M[1..m] register array (ASP313.1, ASP313.5). Same conceptual step, slightly different data structure size. Composite L2-vs-L2 entry permitted under the parent-first allowance because both parent algorithms are matched above.

Streaming update loop. Both: hash each record, peel off first b bits to address the bucket, update per-bucket structure with rho applied to the remainder. FM sets BITMAP[alpha, rho(...)] = 1; HLL sets M[j] = max(M[j], rho(w)). The set-bit-once vs take-max distinction is the algorithmic essence of the FM->HLL refinement (max keeps only one int per bucket vs FM's L-bit bitmap).

Aggregate-and-return steps. FM scans each BITMAP row to find its R^{(i)}, sums to S, and outputs trunc(m/phi * 2^{S/m}). HLL computes Z = (sum_j 2^{-M[j]})^{-1} (harmonic-mean aggregate) and returns alpha_m m^2 Z. Same role (per-bucket observable -> aggregate -> exponentiate -> bias-correct) with FM's geometric-mean-via-arithmetic-mean-of-logs replaced by HLL's harmonic-mean.

Main bias-and-standard-error theorem of each paper. FM's Theorem 5: bias ~ 1 + 0.31/m, standard error ~ 0.78/sqrt(m). HLL's Theorem 1: bias asymptotically 1 (with delta_1 < 5e-5 for m>=16), standard error beta_m/sqrt(m) with beta_infty = sqrt(3 log 2 - 1) approx 1.03896. Same THEOREM structure (asymptotic moments of the estimator at fixed m, with periodic-fluctuation control of order 1e-5), different constants reflecting the different aggregation rules. HLL's main quantitative contribution is replacing FM's 0.78 with 1.04 while collapsing register width from L bits to log_2 log_2 N bits.

The asymptotic constants alpha_m -> 1/(2 log 2) approx 0.72134 and beta_m -> sqrt(3 log 2 - 1) approx 1.03896 (HLL EP313.6) are the analogues of FM's bias factor 1+0.31/m and standard-error constant sigma_infty/sqrt(m) approx 0.78/sqrt(m). The mathematical role - leading-order asymptotic constants extracted from a Mellin-pole calculation - is the same; the values differ because of the harmonic-vs-arithmetic-mean choice.

Ideal-multiset hypothesis. Both papers do their analysis under the assumption that hashed values constitute n i.i.d. uniform random variables on [0,1] (equivalently i.i.d. uniform binary strings). HLL's DP313.8 (ideal multiset) plus AssumP313.1 (ideal-multiset hypothesis) parallel FM's DP314.6 (probabilistic model on B) and DP314.7 (R_n on n i.i.d. samples).

Poisson model (HLL DP313.10): HLL replaces fixed-n analysis by a Poisson(lambda) random sample size, then depoissonizes. FM does NOT explicitly use poissonization; it works directly with fixed-n inclusion-exclusion sums. This is a methodological refinement in HLL that has no direct FM counterpart (FM uses Mellin on F(n) directly).

Mellin transform. Both papers cite the same classical definition (FM cites De Bruijn / Knuth AOCP Vol. 3; HLL cites Flajolet-Gourdon-Dumas 1995). External-origin in both papers; the underlying cited result is the same. Carries no relationship signal beyond confirming both use Mellin-based asymptotic analysis.

Geometric distribution of rho. Both papers note that rho(x) for x uniform on B is geometric with P[rho >= k] = 2^{1-k} (HLL EP313.2 explicit; FM DP314.6 implicit in its uniform model on B). Identical fact at the foundation of both analyses.

Mellin-asymptotics machinery applied to the central integral / generating function. HLL's Lemma LP313.1 gives a Mellin expansion of G(x,xu) (the per-bucket-conditioned integrand), with factorization h_u^*(s) = 2^s Gamma(s) ((1+u)^{-s} - (2+u)^{-s}) / (1 - 2^s) in strip <-1,0>. FM's Lemma 2 (LP314.2) gives F^*(s) = Gamma(s) N(s) / (1 - 2^s) in -1 < Re(s) < 0 - exactly the same structure (Gamma factor x Dirichlet-like factor / (1 - 2^s)). The N(s) (Morse-Thue Dirichlet) of FM is morally analogous to the (1+u)^{-s} - (2+u)^{-s} factor of HLL: both encode the discrete bit-pattern combinatorics of rho. The match is analogous because the algebraic forms differ - HLL has an extra integral over u from the harmonic-mean step - but the Mellin-pole-of-1/(1-2^s) mechanism for periodic fluctuations is identical.

Exact closed-form distribution at fixed n. FM's Theorem 1 gives P[R_n >= k] = q_{n,k} via inclusion-exclusion on the disjoint events E_j and K_k. HLL's Proposition PrP313.1 gives a multinomial closed form for E_n(Z), the expectation of the harmonic-mean indicator. Both are the exact-fixed-n starting point of the asymptotic analysis. Type compatibility is high (theorem ~ proposition); they differ because HLL's observable is Z (a sum-of-2^{-M_j}) while FM's is R (leftmost zero), so the closed form involves multinomials in HLL but pure inclusion-exclusion in FM.

Asymptotic mean of the per-bucket observable. FM Theorem 3.A: bar{R}_n = log_2(phi n) + P(log_2 n) + o(1) (Mellin-residue calculation). HLL Proposition PrP313.2 + PrP313.3: E_n(Z) = lambda/(m alpha_m) (1 + epsilon_m + o(1)) via Poisson-then-depoissonize. Both compute the leading asymptotic of the central observable's mean using Mellin-transform-of-F-style calculations; HLL adds a depoissonization step (PrP313.3) that FM avoids by working directly fixed-n.

Proof-of-main-bias-and-variance theorem. HLL's PP313.3 (sketch combining PrP313.2, PrP313.3 for mean and the parallel K(x) machinery for variance) parallels FM's chain PP314.5 (Theorem 3.A) -> PP314.6 (Theorem 3.B) -> PP314.9 (Theorem 4) -> PP314.10 (Theorem 5). Both proofs follow Mellin -> residue-at-pole -> periodic-fluctuation-control. HLL's proof is shorter as a sketch; FM's is broken into more lemmas because every step needs a tail bound (LP314.4, LP314.5, CP314.A1).

Analytic depoissonization (Jacquet-Szpankowski theorem, cited externally in HLL). FM does not depoissonize, so this external-origin cited result has no FM counterpart. Listed for completeness even though external; flagged as paper-internal-significant because HLL's whole asymptotic machinery hinges on it.

Variance machinery. HLL's EP313.7 introduces K(x) = x^2 integral u G(x,xu)^m du as the integral form of E_{P(lambda)}(Z^2); EP313.8 gives the asymptotic Poisson variance; EP313.9 depoissonizes to V_n(Z) = V_{P(n)}(Z) + O(n). FM's Theorem 3.B (TP314.3b) and its proof PP314.6 give sigma_n^2 = sigma_infty^2 + Q(log_2 n) + o(1) via a triple-pole Mellin residue at s=0 of G(n) = sum k^2 psi(n/2^k) - F(n)^2. Same role (variance asymptotics via Mellin of an explicit integral/sum), different aggregation rule, so analogous.

Identity 1/a = integral_0^infty e^{-at} dt (used by HLL's PSP313.1 to decouple the harmonic-mean factor (sum 2^{-k_j})^{-1}). FM has no analogous step because its observable R is not a harmonic mean - this identity is the technical key to handling HLL's harmonic averaging and is genuinely new vs FM. Origin: external (elementary calculus); listed as none because it is the methodological hinge of the HLL refinement.

HLL remark on the arithmetic nature of alpha_m and beta_m (rational combinations of log 2, zeta values, polylogs at 1/2). FM's analogous remark would concern the arithmetic structure of phi and sigma_infty via N(s), but this is not articulated as a separate node in paper 314. Paper-original to HLL.

Memory rule. HLL RP313.2: register width log_2 log_2 N + O(1) bits (e.g. m=2048, 32-bit hash, 5-bit registers gives ~1.5 kB for n up to 10^9 at 2% accuracy). FM RP314.2: BITMAP length L > log_2(n/m) + 4 (e.g. nmap=64, L=16 supports n up to 10^5; L=24 covers n >> 10^7) - i.e. L = O(log N). Same role (storage budget per bucket), different scaling: HLL is the headline log_2 log_2 N improvement over FM's log_2 N.

Distributed/parallel implementation via componentwise combination of register vectors. HLL: combine register vectors by max. FM: combine BITMAPs by OR. Both are commutative, associative, and idempotent (hence partition-invariant), giving the same conclusion: communication O(s) messages, accuracy unaffected by partition. This is the streaming/distributed-folklore property and matches exactly.

Storage/accuracy lower bound. FM's open problem OpenP314.1 (1985) explicitly asks whether better than O(m log_2 n) storage with c/sqrt(m) error is possible. HLL's remarks RP313.4 (info-theoretic Omega(log log N) lower bound on register width) and RP313.5 (cited Chassaing-Gerin 2006 lower bound on accuracy ~ 1/sqrt(m)) RESOLVE the FM open problem in the affirmative for storage (yes, log log N suffices) and tightly upper-bound the accuracy gap: HLL is within 4% of the order-statistics lower bound. The FM `resolves` edge in the FM JSON points TP314.5 -> OpenP314.1, and HLL's RP313.4/RP313.5 close the loop.

Direct identity match via citation: HLL's AP313.4 (origin: external, citation Flajolet & Martin 1985) IS paper 314's AP314.3 (PCSA). HLL cites FM's relative accuracy as 0.78/sqrt(m), which matches FM's TP314.5 conclusion. This is the strongest direct edge between the two papers and the primary signal that the relation_type is EXT (HLL's contribution is positioned exactly as a refinement of this cited FM result).

LogLog (Durand-Flajolet 2003), 1.30/sqrt(m) accuracy, geometric-mean-based. External-origin in HLL with no FM counterpart (it postdates FM by 18 years and is the immediate predecessor of HLL within the same algorithmic lineage).

MinCount (Bar-Yossef et al. 2002 / Giroire 2005, 2006), order-statistics-based with 1.00/sqrt(m) accuracy. External-origin in HLL, no FM counterpart - it is a different design point in the cardinality-estimator zoo.
Adaptive Sampling (Flajolet 1990), 1.20/sqrt(m). External-origin in HLL, no FM counterpart (postdates FM 1985).

Hit Counting / linear counting (Whang-Vander-Zanden-Taylor 1990): bitmap of size N/10, n approx m log(m/V). External-origin in HLL, no FM counterpart. Used inside HLL's small-range correction (ASP313.8) but not present in FM.

FM's basic COUNT procedure (single-BITMAP, no stochastic averaging). HLL has no analogous primitive - it never describes a single-register estimator separately. AP314.1 is the conceptual stepping stone within paper 314 toward PCSA but is not part of the HLL design.

FM's Direct-averaging algorithm (m independent hash functions, O(m) hashing cost per record). HLL has no such variant - HLL exclusively uses stochastic averaging. AP314.2 is paper 314's intermediate construct showing why stochastic averaging is needed.
FM's bit function bit(y,k) is a low-level helper for the BITMAP indexing; HLL does not introduce an equivalent named primitive. Paper-original to FM but trivially familiar.

FM's nu(n) = popcount used to build the Morse-Thue Dirichlet generating function N(s). HLL's Mellin analysis routes through different building blocks (the (1+u)^{-s} - (2+u)^{-s} factor in EP313.5), so there is no nu-based machinery in HLL.

FM's definition of standard error and bias (sigma(hat n)/n; lim E[hat n]/n). HLL uses these notions but does not promote them to numbered definition nodes - they appear inline in TP313.1. Treating as paper-original to FM at the JSON-node level.

Auxiliary functions psi(x) = sum (-1)^{nu(j)+1} e^{-jx}, F(x) = sum_{k>=1} psi(x/2^k), and N(s) = Dirichlet of Morse-Thue signs. These three are FM's Mellin building blocks, with no HLL analogue: HLL's f(u) = log_2((2+u)/(1+u)) plays a parallel role, but the explicit Morse-Thue connection (alternating signs from leftmost-zero combinatorics) does not appear in HLL because HLL's observable is max not leftmost-zero.

FM's auxiliary Mellin estimates: Lemma 3 bounds N(s); Appendix lemma and corollary bound f(x,t) and N(it) on the imaginary axis. HLL does not need these because its Mellin factor is rational in (1+u)^{-s}, (2+u)^{-s} rather than the Morse-Thue Dirichlet. Paper-original FM technical lemmas with no HLL counterpart.

FM Lemma 4 (asymptotic of E[beta^{R_n}] via Mellin pole at s = -1/q) and Lemma 5 (concentration of bucket loads via binomial unimodality). HLL replaces both with the cleaner Poisson model + Jacquet-Szpankowski depoissonization, which removes the need for explicit bucket-load concentration arguments. These are paper-original FM lemmas obsoleted by HLL's methodology.

FM Theorem 1 (closed-form q_{n,k} via inclusion-exclusion) and Theorem 2 (three-regime asymptotics for q_{n,k} including the limiting profile psi(n/2^k)). HLL works with Z directly via its own integral form rather than going through P[R_n >= k]; PrP313.1 is the closest HLL analogue (already matched above) but FM's per-regime tail-bound machinery has no direct HLL counterpart - HLL outsources tail bounds to the depoissonization theorem TP313.2.

FM's Theorems 3.A (mean of R_n with the magic constant phi) and 3.B (sigma of R_n with sigma_infty = 1.12127). These are subsumed (analogously) by HLL's PrP313.2 + PrP313.3 + the variance counterparts EP313.8, EP313.9, all of which were matched above. Listing here additionally as none would duplicate; instead they are absorbed by the analogous matches above. (No new none entries emitted.)

FM Theorem 4 (closed-form asymptotics for E[E_n], E[E_n^2] of PCSA via Gamma(-1/m), N(-1/m), N(-2/m)). HLL has no direct analogue at this level because its harmonic-mean estimator does not factor through a power E[2^{S/m}]; HLL's parallel role is split across PrP313.2 (mean of Z) and EP313.7-EP313.9 (variance of Z), already matched. Including as a separate none entry to satisfy the completeness check that every L1 paper-origin node appears.

FM remark on standard-error scaling sigma_infty/sqrt(m). The corresponding HLL remark (alpha_m -> 1/(2 log 2), beta_m -> sqrt(3 log 2 - 1)) is captured in EP313.6, already matched. No new HLL counterpart needed.

FM bias-correction-for-small-m remark: replace varphi by varphi(1 + 0.31/m) in the final estimator. HLL's analogue would be its empirical small-range linear-counting correction (ASP313.8 inside AP313.2), which serves a different purpose (small-cardinality regime, not small-m). Paper-original FM detail; no clean HLL match.
FM scrolling encoding remark (encode only the BITMAP fringe to save storage). Specific to FM's BITMAP data structure; HLL's compact register array makes this trick irrelevant.
FM remark on supporting deletions via per-pattern counters. HLL has no deletion discussion and the trick (turn each BITMAP bit into a counter) is FM-specific.
